subject: How to summaries multivariate posterior distributions

messages.author: fcf931fd673ef552
messages.subject: How to summaries multivariate posterior distributions
parts:
Hi 

I have a unit simplex parameter. Which is given a dirichlet(1,1,1) prior. 

parameters{
    simplex[3] W;
........
}
model{
   W ~ dirichlet(alpha);
 .........
}

What is the best way to get summaries of the posterior distribution of W ?

Marginal distributions are misleading, specially the Intervals. 

Thank you very much for any help. 

Best regards
Sreenath Madathil

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to summaries multivariate posterior distributions
parts:
A Dirichlet(1) prior is uniform, so you don't even need
the sampling statement, as variables get uniform priors by
default.

With only 3 outcomes, the triangle/ternary plot is typical:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_plot

I think there are built-ins for this in R, but I don't know
about Python or other languages.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to summaries multivariate posterior distributions
parts:
Hi Bob, 

Thank you very much for the reply. 
I am currently using the ternary plot using ggtern in R.
However, in my field of work readers are more familiar with 95% intervals. 
How could I get joint intervals and point summaries?

I understand from reading from discussions this group that,  
Posterior mean minimizes expected squared errors and  Posterior median minimizes expected absolute errors. 
And I can get posterior multivariate mode  by using the mode of log posterior. 

However, I would like to report multivariate posterior mode/median with an 95% or 80% interval around it. 

Something like (see also the image):

         2.5%  97.5%           2.5%  97.5%
W1    0.80    0.20              0.40    0.48

W2    0.15    0.70              0.40    0.48

W3    0.05    0.10              0.20    0.04


Thank you
Best regards
Sreenath Madathil

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to summaries multivariate posterior distributions
parts:
95% intervals require a lot of samples and are more sensitive
to priors than more central intervals, so use them with caution.
We're about to change our defaults to drop the 95% interval print outs.

I don't know what a 95% posterior interval is and don't understand
your example that seems ot have a lower value for 97.5% than 2.5%?
And there are two lines per variable.

- Bob
